one_liner: Import-swap replacement for Go's encoding/json; unmarshalled typed structs ~2x faster than encoding/json in one third-party benchmark.
what_it_does: A JSON encoder/decoder for Go with the same API as encoding/json: Marshal/Unmarshal, Encoder/Decoder, Marshaler/Unmarshaler, RawMessage, Number, Valid/Compact/Indent and the same struct-tag rules. Switching means changing the import path. It also offers options encoding/json lacks: context.Context passed into MarshalJSON/UnmarshalJSON, colorized output, type-safe field filtering, unsorted map output (UnorderedMap) and first-key-wins decoding. Unreleased master adds generic MarshalOf/UnmarshalOf, which keep the caller's value off the heap.
how_it_is_fast: Instead of walking values with reflect on every call, it compiles a decoder per type, and for encoding a linear opcode program run by a switch-dispatch VM that fuses opcodes and handles recursion as a jump, both cached by the type's runtime pointer ("typeptr") and looked up without a lock. The decoder copies the input into a NUL-terminated buffer so scan loops need no end-of-buffer check, and reads bytes through unsafe pointers to skip bounds checks. In v0.10.x, the version benchmarked, struct keys are matched with per-character bitmaps (up to 16 fields, keys under 64 bytes) and decoded strings point into that buffer instead of being copied. Unreleased master replaces this with AVX2/NEON 64-byte block scanning to skip values (prefix-XOR quote masks, popcount bracket counting), a hash table of case-folded keys compared 8 bytes at a time, and one-pass number parsing (Clinger's fast path plus a 128-bit power-of-ten table).
when_to_use: Services that Unmarshal into concrete Go structs, including nested map[string]T and slices of structs, and want roughly 2x over encoding/json by changing one import. The measured case was multi-MB documents (5 SEC files, 39.9 MB total).
Decode throughput at low to moderate parallelism: in the same harness it matched or beat sonic at 1-4 threads (90.8 vs 86.1 MB/s at 1 thread, 200.1 vs 180.2 MB/s at 4 threads).
Codebases that need encoding/json semantics but won't add code generation (easyjson) or learn a different API.
Portable builds: v0.10.x has no assembly, so it compiles on any GOARCH that Go supports. Master adds SIMD paths with a word-at-a-time fallback, and its CI runs on Linux, macOS and Windows.
Code that wants context.Context passed into custom (Un)MarshalJSON methods, or JSON field filtering, which encoding/json doesn't provide.
when_not_to_use: Untrusted or malformed input on the released v0.10.6: open issues report index-out-of-range panics (#604, where decoder state carries over between calls, and #609) and a fatal checkptr crash (#575) where encoding/json returns an error. The fixes exist only on untagged master.

Memory-tight processes: peak RSS was 227 vs 158 MB at 1 thread and 409 vs 328 MB at 8 threads against encoding/json. v0.10.x copies the whole input on each call, and decoded strings keep that copy alive.
Structs with more than 16 fields that rely on case-insensitive key matching in v0.10.x: fields can silently stay empty (#427, open).
Token-by-token streaming with Decoder.Token(): an open issue (#396) reports up to ~50x slower than encoding/json on some files and ~90 MB of memory to walk a 50 MB file.

Teams that can't absorb toolchain breakage or unreleased code. v0.10.x hooks into runtime/reflect internals with dozens of go:linkname directives, and one of them broke against Go 1.23 dev (#506). The linkname-free master was largely rewritten between 20 and 25 Sept 2026 (PR bodies say 'Generated with Claude Code') and has no tag.

integration.min_toolchain: go.mod says Go 1.19 for v0.10.5/v0.10.6 and Go 1.21 on master; master CI tests only Go 1.25, 1.26 and 1.27
integration.platforms: any GOOS/GOARCH for v0.10.x (pure Go plus unsafe). Master adds AVX2 scanners on amd64 (detected at runtime via CPUID/XGETBV) and NEON on arm64, with a word-at-a-time fallback elsewhere
integration.thread_safety: Package-level Marshal/Unmarshal are meant to be called concurrently: per-call contexts come from a pool and type caches are shared without locks (README). v0.10.5 has an open data-race report in the type compiler's non-race build path (#566). The fix (#567, July 2026) is on master only and in no release.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same function names, types and struct-tag rules, so switching is an import swap. Open v0.10.x issues document divergences, though: interface decoding (#443), MarshalJSON handling (#418), case-insensitive keys on structs with more than 16 fields (#427), and panics or fatal errors instead of returned errors on some malformed input (#575, #604).

gotchas: The benchmark measured v0.10.5, and `go get` today resolves v0.10.6, which adds one bug fix. The large decoder/encoder rewrite (SIMD scanning, key table, UnmarshalOf, linkname removal) is untagged master. Its speed claims, such as beating sonic on struct decoding, come from the author's own CI, not a release.

In v0.10.x, decoded strings point into an internal copy of the whole input, so keeping any decoded string keeps the entire document copy alive (described in PR #658). Master copies strings into shared buffers of up to 16 KB by default. DecodeNoCopyString makes strings alias the caller's input, which must then not be modified.

MarshalOf/UnmarshalOf (master only) work on a pooled copy and copy the result back. That makes large values slower, and UnmarshalJSON/UnmarshalText methods must not keep the receiver's address. MarshalNoEscape/UnmarshalNoEscape are deprecated as unsafe when a goroutine stack moves, and now behave like the plain calls.

Heavy unsafe use even after the linkname removal: master reads string-keyed maps by reinterpreting map[K]V as map[string][n]uint64. That relies on the runtime's map layout, with separate go1.24 and pre-go1.24 build variants, so a future change to Go's maps could break it.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over jsoniter when you want the faster and more compatible drop-in: in the same harness it beat jsoniter at every thread count (90.8 vs 79.3 MB/s at 1 thread, 256.7 vs 233.6 at 8 threads), and its README calls jsoniter only partially encoding/json-compatible. Pick it over Sonic at 1-4 threads or where you want no JIT (sonic edged it at 8 threads, 260.0 vs 256.7 MB/s, with 320 vs 409 MB peak RSS), and over easyjson when you can't add a code-generation step.
verified_claims_summary: In the third-party tegridy-benchie harness (i7-6820HQ, 4 cores/8 threads; Go 1.27.1 or later, exact patch not recorded; plain go build), go-json v0.10.5 decoded 5 SEC companyfacts files (39.9 MB) into typed structs with nested maps, plus the same fact reduction, at 90.8 MB/s vs encoding/json 44.5 MB/s at 1 thread (~2.0x) and 256.7 vs 128.8 MB/s at 8 threads (~2.0x), using more peak memory. The baseline is Go 1.27's encoding/json, which go-json's option docs describe as built on encoding/json/v2, and the timings include the shared reduction step, which dilutes the parse-only ratio.
status_note: An MIT, dependency-free Go module usable via `go get`, active again but unreleased: only two commits landed between v0.10.5 (Jan 2025) and 20 Sept 2026, v0.10.6 (Mar 2026) holds a single fix, and dozens of large performance and compatibility PRs merged to master between 20 and 25 Sept 2026 without a tag.
